findings.claim: The second module gap's justification explains one dropped item, not a module with zero items. React auth-and-review is taught in full on both tracks: calendar S34 and FT19 list 'Login with a session cookie or JWT', 'Protected pages and role-based screens', 'Handling 401 and 403: redirect and sign out' and 'Turning off the dev profile', none marked (skim). Its objectives are client-side behaviour that q08 does not test. handling-401-and-403-redirect-and-sign-out o2/o3: on 401, clear auth state and redirect to login; on 403, show not-allowed and keep the session. protected-pages-and-role-based-screens o1/o3: a Navigate route guard, and the fact that front-end guards only shape the UI. login-with-a-session-cookie-or-jwt o3: credentials: 'include' or a Bearer header. q08 only tests how the Spring resource server maps a token to a 401/403/200 status. Even if the dropped item really did duplicate q08, any of those objectives could have replaced it. Line 46 sits right next to it, and the other gap there (integration-and-observability: FT8 integration test and RestClient (skim), FT5 logging (skim), health checks on no FT day) is truly scope-based. Read together, the two lines suggest both gaps are forced by scope, but this one is a choice the author made. It leaves out a full module that is also a core Project 2 feature.
findings.recommendation: Minimum fix (documentation only, no bank change): rewrite line 47 to say the module is taught in full on both tracks and was left out by choice when its one candidate item overlapped q08. Name the module's untested objectives so the owner can see the gap. Optional, owner's call because it reopens an accepted bank: replace one React item (q22, so components-and-state keeps q21) with a 401-versus-403 client-handling trace or a route-guard item. That keeps 6 React items and 30 in total.

findings.claim: The overrun default rests on a precedent the repository does not support. The md says the Foundation checkpoint 'already does' this on F30, 'where 180 minutes of checkpoint rows (90 MCQ + 90 coding) replace the 120-minute Gate block'. In git grep on this branch and on main, no tracked file except the calendar mentions F30, and nothing records a 180-minute or 90 + 90 F30 ledger. The calendar's F30 is dayType Gate, the same single 120-minute 'Proctored assessment' block as S43. The figure seems to come from an off-repo Foundation taxonomy workbook planning row, and 'replace the 120-minute Gate block' interprets that row. It is also not a like-for-like precedent. F30's assessment record lists MCQ as a format and weights it (mcq 24), so its MCQ was a scored part of the gate. S43/FT25's Final record lists no MCQ format and no MCQ weight. An owner would read the 60 + T overrun as established practice for an equivalent case, and it is neither.
findings.recommendation: Cite the actual source (the workbook name and revision, and the row), call it an off-repo planning figure, and drop 'already does' unless a tracked ledger records it. Add that F30's MCQ is weighted and the S43/FT25 checkpoint is not. Give a source for the line-102 coding mix 'two Spring Boot, one Python, one Docker or second Python', or mark it as planned.

findings.claim: The md calls the default 'reversible', but the blueprint's learner-facing instructions fix it: 'taken ... as the first sitting of the proctored Final day'. So any owner reorder means editing learner text. The md also does not weigh the cost of the order. Learners spend the first 60 proctored minutes on an unweighted MCQ (blueprint weights {}), then take the weighted no-AI coding (calendar aiOffCoding 32). When T > 60 that coding also runs past the 120-minute day type every calendar day uses. MCQ-first does follow the calendar's own Gate wording, 'MCQ + coding assessment', so the order is defensible. It is just not argued, and 'rejected alternatives' (line 112) does not consider running coding first.
findings.recommendation: Reword the instructions to drop 'first' (for example 'a sitting of the proctored Final day'), so the order can change without editing learner text. Add one line to the md giving the reason for MCQ-first (the calendar's Gate wording), and note the fatigue trade-off with the weighted coding when T > 60.

findings.claim: The 8/5/7/6/4 split is defensible, but no rule for it is recorded. The table shows days and item counts only. Against taught time, Spring Boot is slightly under-sampled: 13 of 39 Standard days (33%) and 8 of 23 Fast days (35%), but 8 of 30 items (27%). Python is slightly over: 6/39 (15%) and 3/23 (13%), but 5 items (17%). By fully taught topic count the gaps are within one item (Spring about 9, Python about 4, HTML/CSS/JS about 7, React about 6, Containers about 4), so the split is acceptable. A reviewer cannot tell that from the md, though.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence giving the allocation rule. For example: proportional to topics taught in full on both tracks, then adjusted so every in-scope module has at least one item, with the Spring -1 / Python +1 difference explained.

findings.claim: The learner-facing instructions say the checkpoint 'covers content taught in full on both tracks'. Yet objectives line 47 lists image-layers-and-build-caching#o2 as assessed, and that topic is a Reading on S36 and '(skim)' on FT21. The md's Scope (line 37) puts Fast-skim topics out of scope. The q27 exception is fair overall: the multi-stage-builds page, taught in full on S36/FT21, shows the exact dependency-first build stage (COPY mvnw pom.xml ./, COPY .mvn .mvn, RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline, COPY src ./src), and distractors A and B are rejected by multi-stage facts (a JRE has no JDK for Maven; the build stage needs a JDK). One md claim goes further than that. Line 41 says 'every distractor is rejected with multi-stage facts', but distractor D (.dockerignore src) relies on .dockerignore, which only the image-layers page teaches (its objective o3); the multi-stage and containers-and-images pages never mention it. A Fast learner can still reject D by common sense, since the build then has no sources, as the feedback says.
findings.recommendation: Keep q27. Change md line 41 to say A and B are rejected with multi-stage facts and D because the build would have no sources. Optionally soften the instructions to 'covers content taught on both tracks', or note in Scope that the image-layers objective is listed only as the documented q27 exception.

findings.claim: The ledger quotes the Gate format as 'MCQ + coding assessment'. The calendar's dayTypes.Gate.blocks[0].evolvFormat is 'MCQ + coding assessment (walkthrough recording pending in Evolv)'. The dropped parenthetical bears on the md's next claim, that the walkthrough uses no Final-day minutes. That claim does hold: S42 is 'Walkthrough rehearsal and recording' and FT24 includes 'Walkthrough rehearsal and recording'. The other ledger facts check out against the calendar: the Gate block is 120 minutes; the Final record lists formats coding, capstone (auto-graded) and recorded walkthrough, with weights aiOffCoding 32, capstone 24, communication 8, moduleChecks 20 and walkthrough 16, cut scores pool 70 and tierA 85, and no MCQ weight.
findings.recommendation: Quote the full evolvFormat string and add that the 'walkthrough recording pending in Evolv' note refers to the S42/FT24 recording, not to Final-day minutes.

findings.claim: The blueprint sets passMark 70 with empty weights, and the instructions tell learners the score 'is reported against a 70 percent readiness mark'. The sitting is on the programme's last day, so it does not say what the learner is being judged ready for, or what happens below 70 (no retake, no gating, no report recipient). Learners may read 70 as a pass/fail gate on the Final. The md (lines 115-117) says the defaults set no certification policy, but the learner text does not.
findings.recommendation: State the consequence in the instructions, for example: 'diagnostic only; reported to your instructor; no pass or fail effect on the Final'. Or name what readiness the mark refers to.

findings.claim: q17 partly overlaps the in-progress HTML/CSS/JS course-final q05 (fm/pep-course-ending-html-css-js: html-css-js/assessments/web-client-mcq/final-mcq.gift). Both are let-loop closure traces that multiply i, and both turn on the same fact: let gives each iteration its own i. q17's distractor 90 ('one shared i ending at 3') is the same misconception as q05's '40, 40, 40'. That fact is also the formative scope-and-closures artifact.gift item 'o3 loop with let' and the javascript-fundamentals practice item 'scope-and-closures o3 from symptom to fix'. The setups differ (an array of handlers with map/filter/reduce, versus setTimeout with a variable read late), and q17 adds a filter/reduce step, so this is not 'same setup + same deciding fact'. A learner who sits both finals will still meet the per-iteration-let fact as the main decision twice. The md's lexical result (highest Jaccard, q17 against web-final q01) does not reveal this conceptual neighbour.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable as is for a cumulative checkpoint. When the HTML/CSS/JS course-final pin is final, have the duplication critic judge q17 against web-final q05 explicitly. If the owner wants less overlap, move q17's deciding fact toward its second objective (reduce with an explicit initial value) rather than the loop binding.
